newsitem.title: INDIA: India company panel outlines share buyback plan.
newsitem.headline: India company panel outlines share buyback plan.

text.p: A working group set up by the government recommended on Monday that Indian companies be allowed to buy back their own shares subject to certain conditions.
The report, which considered amendments to the Companies Act, said current laws which prevented share buybacks were "antiquated" and went against the interest of shareholders.
"In today's context, the group strongly believes this section (of the Act) is antiquated, and goes against the long-term interests of corporate sector growth and shareholder value," the report said.
It recommended that shareholders must approve a proposed buyback through a special resolution which states the amount allocated, and the time frame, for the buyback.
The funds allocated for the buyback must be from the firm's "free reserves" and share premium account, the report said.
Firms which have issued shares at a premium to their face value usually deposit the funds in a separate account.

Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in his budget proposals for 1997/98 (April-March) said last week that buybacks of shares would be allowed under a new company law for which a legislative bill would be introduced in parliament.
Chidambaram set up the working group last year under the chairmanship of K. R. Chandratre, the then chairman of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India to present a report for public debate.
The group said companies must not be allowed to issue any new shares -- including rights shares but excluding bonus shares -- for one year after the buyback was completed.
"Since a buyback is for extinguishing share capital it should not lead to an increase in the debt-equity ratio in excess of 2:1," the report said.
It said in the case of a buyback that would constitute a treasury operation, new shares should not be re-issued for a period of two years.

If a company's treasury department buys its own shares as an investment it would qualify as a treasury operation. In the case of a "full buy-out" -- where a person or group acquires 95 percent of a publicly listed company either through a takeover or otherwise -- the report said shareholders should be allowed to sell their shares at a price based on guidelines set by the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the market regulator.
